en: Kālidāsa: For the comprehension of both word and meaning, I salute Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord, the parents of the world, who are joined together like word and meaning. (Raghuvamśa 1.1)
Where is the lineage originating from the Sun, and where is my intellect of such limited scope?
Out of delusion, I desire to cross the impassable ocean with a mere raft.
Dull-witted though I am, yet desiring the fame of a poet, I shall fall into ridicule—
like a dwarf who, out of greed for a fruit reachable only by the tall, stretches out his arms.
Or rather, since the gateway of speech has been opened for this lineage by former sages,
my way of entry is like that of a thread through a gem already perforated by a diamond.
Thus, [I shall describe] those kings whose purity began from birth, whose actions bore fruit until their completion,
who ruled the earth as far as the ocean, and whose chariot tracks reached to the very mines of the earth.

They had offered oblations into the sacred fires according to the prescribed rites; they honored supplicants according to their desires; they meted out punishments according to the offenses committed; and they remained awake at their appointed times.
For those who have accumulated wealth for the sake of giving; for those who speak measuredly for the sake of truth;
for those desiring victory for the sake of glory; and for householders for the sake of progeny.
Having mastered the sciences in childhood, seeking the objects of the senses in youth,
adopting the conduct of sages in old age, and finally casting off the body through yoga at the end.
Though my power of speech is meager, I shall recount the lineage of the Raghus,
having been deceived into rashness by their virtues as they reached my ears.
The virtuous, who are the means for discerning the real from the unreal, ought to hear this;
for in fire, both the purity and the dross of gold are clearly perceived.
The son of Vivasvat named Manu was the first among the rulers of the earth, as worthy of honor among the wise as the syllable Om (praṇava) is among the Vedic meters.
In that pure lineage was born one even purer,
named Dilīpa, a moon among kings, like the moon born from the ocean of milk.
Broad-chested, with shoulders like those of a bull, tall as a *sāla* tree, and long-armed,
he possessed a body capable of performing his own duties, as if he were the very dharma of the warrior caste incarnate.
With a body that surpassed all others in essence, eclipsed all splendors,
and rose above everything, he stood upon the earth as if he were Mount Meru itself.
His wisdom was equal to his appearance; his learning was equal to his wisdom;
his undertakings were equal to his learning; and his success was equal to his undertakings.
By means of his royal qualities, which were both formidable and attractive,
he was both unassailable and approachable to his dependents, just as the ocean is both unapproachable and accessible because of its marine treasures.
Not even by so much as a hair’s breadth did his subjects ever deviate from the path of their own duty, which he had trodden; they moved like the wheels of a chariot under the guidance of that driver.
For the sake of the prosperity of his subjects alone, he accepted tribute from them;
for the sun draws up moisture only to release it back a thousandfold.
His army and his equipment—these two alone were the means for accomplishing his goals;
his intellect was engaged in the sacred scriptures, and his bowstring was drawn upon his bow.
The undertakings of that king, who kept his counsel secret and concealed his outward gestures and internal intentions,
could only be inferred from their results, much like the latent impressions (saṃskāras) of a previous life.
Fearless, he protected himself; free from ailment, he practiced dharma;
without greed, he acquired wealth; and unattached, he experienced happiness.
Silence in wisdom, forbearance in power, and the absence of self-praise in renunciation—
these virtues of his seemed as if they were siblings, for each was bound to the others.
Unattracted by sense objects and having reached the further shore of the sciences,
he, who delighted in dharma, attained old age without the physical decay of senility.
Because he disciplines, instructs, protects, and sustains his subjects, he is their father;
their biological fathers are merely the causes of their birth.

For that wise king, even his pursuit of wealth and pleasure was rooted solely in righteousness: in punishing those deserving of punishment for the sake of maintaining order, and in marrying for the sake of procreation.
That Maghavan milked the earth for sacrifice and the heavens for grain;
through the exchange of their respective riches, they both sustained the two worlds.
It is said that other kings could not equal the fame of that protector,
since thievery— though established in the scriptures— had turned away from the property of others.
To him who was thus afflicted, even a learned man, though disliked, was esteemed as medicine;
whereas a wicked person, though beloved, was to be shunned like a snake that has bitten the thumb.
Surely the Creator fashioned him through the meditative absorption of the great elements;
for indeed, all his qualities had as their sole fruit the welfare of others.
He ruled the earth, which had the ocean as its moat and the coastal regions as its ramparts,
as if it were a single city, under his undisputed command.
He had a wife born of the Magadha lineage named Sudakṣiṇā, so called because of her innate courtesy; she was like the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of a ritual.

The lord of the earth considered himself possessed of a wife by virtue of that high-minded lady, even though he already had a vast harem, just as one considers oneself possessed of fortune through the presence of Lakṣmī.
Longing for the birth of a son from her who was worthy of himself,
he passed his time with desires whose fulfillment was long delayed.
Just as Bhagīratha entrusted the Gaṅgā— capable of purifying his ancestors—
to his ministers when he desired offspring, so did he entrust Kosala to them.
Then, having worshipped the Creator with self-restraint out of a desire for a son,
the couple went to the hermitage of their preceptor Vasiṣṭha.
They mounted a single chariot that emitted a smooth and deep resonance,
like lightning and Airāvata ascending a rain-cloud of the monsoon season.
Fearing lest there be any disturbance to the hermitage,
they were accompanied by only a limited number of attendants, like two lordly elephants followed by a small herd of scent-elephants and young calves.
They were served by breezes pleasant to the touch, fragrant with the resin of *sāla* trees,
scattering the pollen of flowers, and shaking the rows of forest groves.
Because the wind was favorable, foretelling the fulfillment of their prayers,
the dust kicked up by the horses did not touch the curls or the head-dresses of the two.
Taking fresh butter, they approached the elders of the cowherd settlement and asked for the names of the wild trees along the path.
In the lakes, they inhaled the fragrance of the lotuses, cooled by the agitation of the waves,
which resembled their own breath.
Delighting their minds, they listened as the peacocks, with heads upturned toward the sound of the chariot wheels,
uttered cries divided into two kinds that harmonized with the *ṣaḍja* note.
They gazed at pairs of deer, whose eyes resembled one another's, as they had recently left the path and were now fixed their sights upon the chariot.
In some places, with their faces raised by cranes whose sweet-sounding cries formed a pillarless archway of floral garlands through their flight in rows; Ragh(K)_1.44.
In the villages established by themselves, marked by sacrificial posts,
they received from the sacrificers unfailing blessings that followed upon their respectful offerings.

As those two, dressed in pure white garments, proceeded together, they possessed a certain indescribable splendor, like the conjunction of the moon with the constellation Citrā when freed from the clouds of winter.
Pointing out various local rulers to his wife, the handsome King Priyadarśana—
resembling a Buddha in wisdom— did not even perceive that the journey had been completed.
Having attained a fame difficult to acquire, he reached the hermitage in the evening with his weary horses,
accompanied by the queen of that great seer who was then observing the vow of restraint.
It was being filled with ascetics returning from the depths of the forest, carrying fuel and kusha grass suspended from their shoulders,
who were purified by the fire that rose to meet them.

At the edge of the watering-place, where the trees had been cleared away by the daughters of the sages for the sake of providing water to the basins from which the birds might drink to their heart's content;
In the courtyards of the leaf-huts, where the wild rice had been gathered as the heat of the sun subsided,
deer were sitting and chewing their cud.
It was crowded with deer accustomed to receiving their share of wild grain, which blocked the doors of the hermits’ huts as if they were their own offspring.
He was purifying those hermits who were setting out toward their guest-huts with clouds of smoke— fragrant with oblations and stirred by the wind— which bore the signs of fires that had been kindled.
Then, having instructed the charioteer to let the draft animals rest,
he helped his wife descend from the chariot and descended himself.

To him, the protector who was accompanied by his wife, those sages— whose senses were most perfectly guarded— performed the rites of hospitality, for he was worthy of such honor and possessed the eye of political wisdom.
At the conclusion of his evening rites, he beheld that treasure-house of asceticism seated beside Arundhatī,
like the consumer of oblations (Agni) beside Svāhā.
The King and the Queen of Magadha grasped their feet;
the preceptor and his wife greeted them with affection in return.
The hospitable sage questioned that sage of the royal order— who had dispelled the fatigue of his journey through hospitality— concerning the welfare of his kingdom.
Then, in the presence of that Atharvanic sage who had conquered the cities of his enemies,
the Lord of Wealth— the best among speakers— uttered these meaningful words.
Is it not indeed fitting that prosperity has come to me, since you are the one who shall avert both divine and human calamities for my seven limbs?
By your mantras, which restrain enemies from afar,
my arrows— though they pierce their visible targets— are as it were repelled.
O Hotṛ priest, the oblation offered by you according to the rules into the fires becomes rain for the crops that have been withered by drought.
The fact that my subjects live out a full human lifespan, free from disease and calamities, is due to the spiritual power of your Brahmanic luster.
Thus, as I am being instructed by my preceptor, the source of the Veda,
how could my prosperity not be free from calamity and accompanied by its necessary consequences?
But since this daughter-in-law of yours has not yet borne a child worthy of her,
even the earth— with its islands and its yield of jewels— does not satisfy me.
Surely, considering me difficult to attain, they have turned their minds toward me;
thus, my ancestors now enjoy the water made warm by their own sighs.
Thus, with my soul purified by sacrifice yet obscured by the failure of progeny,
I am like the mountain Lokāloka— both light and darkness.
Merit arising from austerity and charity brings happiness in other worlds;
however, a lineage of pure descent leads to well-being both in this life and the next.
How is it that the Teacher, beholding me bereft of her, is not pained,
as if looking upon a sapling in the hermitage that has been watered by his own affection yet remains barren?
"O Blessed One, understand my bond of debt to be an unbearable affliction,
like a goad that pierces the vitals of a newly bound elephant."
Therefore, you ought to make such arrangements that I may be liberated;
for regarding this goal so difficult to attain for the Ikṣvākus, success indeed depends upon you.
Thus addressed by the king, the sage, his eyes motionless in meditation,
remained for a moment like a lake whose fish are asleep.
Then he, whose self was cultivated through meditation, perceived by means of his vow the cause of the obstruction to the lineage; he then awakened the Lord of the Earth to this matter.
Formerly, as you were returning to the earth after attending upon Śakra,
Surabhi was waiting for you on the path, resting in the shade of the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
Having remembered that queen after her ritual bath at the end of her menses, he immediately and hastily bypassed the rite of circumambulation, thereby provoking her anger.
"Since you despise me,
you shall have no offspring without first propitiating me"— thus did she curse him.
O King, that curse was heard neither by you nor by the charioteer,
as the celestial Gaṅgā roared while its currents were being agitated by the wild elephants of the quarters.
I understand that my desire depends on his favor;
for the neglect of honoring those worthy of worship obstructs one's spiritual welfare.
That [sacrificial ground] of the wise one, intended for the oblation of a long-duration sacrifice,
now presides over Pātāla, whose gates are closed by serpents.
Therefore, together with your wife, propitiate her—the mother of my child—who is one degree removed from her; she will grant you both your desire.
Even as the Hotṛ priest was speaking thus,
the blameless cow named Nandinī, the means for his sacrificial oblation, returned from the forest.
Bearing a coppery line upon her forehead that was darker than the rest,
she resembled the twilight mingled with the new moon.
The cow with full udders showered the earth with her warm, pure milk, even more purifying than the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*),
as it flowed forth at the mere sight of her calf.
By the particles of dust raised by their hooves that touched his body from close by,
the king felt the purity born of bathing at sacred fords.

Having seen her, whose appearance was auspicious, the ascetic who knew the signs spoke again to his patron, whose prayer had now been made fruitful: *taṃ puṇyadarśanāṃ dṛṣṭvā nimittajñastapodhanaḥ / yājyamāśaṃsitāvandhyaprārthanaṃ punarabravīt //* Ragh(K) 1.85 //
O King, consider that success is not far off for you,
since this auspicious lady has appeared at the very moment her name was uttered.
Subsisting on forest fare, you ought to constantly please this cow by following after her, just as one pleases knowledge through constant practice.
When she has set out, you should set out; when she has halted, you should take up your station;
when she has sat down, you should sit; and when she has drunk water, you should drink water.
And let the devoted daughter-in-law follow her as she departs for the penance grove in the morning after she has been honored, and likewise go out to meet her in the evening.
Until she is pleased, remain devoted to her service;
may you be free from obstacles, and may you stand at the head of those who have sons, like a father.
"So be it," replied the disciple with joy, bowing before his teacher; knowing the proper place and time, he accepted the command along with all its requirements.

Then, at twilight, the son of the Creator, who knew the faults [of the world] and spoke with pleasant truth, dismissed the lord of the people, who possessed exalted splendor, for the sake of retiring to rest.
Although he possessed perfection in asceticism, the sage,
who was skilled in ritual procedures, ordained for him a forest dwelling in accordance with the rules of discipline.

Having occupied the leaf-hut pointed out by the head of the family, he spent the night on a bed of *kuśa* grass with his devoted wife as his sole companion; he lay down there until the end of the night was signaled by the recitation of his pupil.
Thus ends the first canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.

Then at dawn, the lord of subjects, whose wealth was his glory, released for the forest the sage’s cow, from whom he had accepted perfumes and garlands as a gift from his wife, and whose calf had been tied up after drinking its fill.

The lawful wife of the lord of men, who was herself free from worldly passion, followed her path— its dust purified by the placement of her husband's hooves— as Smṛti follows the meaning of Śruti, occupying the foremost place among those worthy of praise.
Having turned back his beloved wife, the compassionate king— fragrant with his own glories—
protected that daughter of Surabhi as if he were protecting the earth itself, which had assumed the form of a cow and whose udders were the four oceans.
By that companion for his vow, even the rest of the retinue was forbidden from following the cow;
yet his protection of the body required no other means, for the progeny of Manu is guarded by its own inherent power.
With mouthfuls of grass that were full of flavor, by scratching her, by warding off gadflies,
and by allowing her unimpeded freedom of movement, the Emperor became intent upon her service.
Standing when she stood, moving when she moved, sitting firm upon his seat when she sat down,
and desiring water when she took water, the king followed her like a shadow.

Bearing royal fortune even though its outward signs had been laid aside— fortune inferred only by his extraordinary majesty— he remained like a lordly elephant in the state of internal rut, whose flow of ichor was not yet manifest.
With his hair entwined by the spreading tendrils of creepers, he roamed the forest with his bow strung,
as if intending to discipline the wild beasts out of malice under the pretext of guarding the sacrificial cow of his preceptor.
As he had dismissed his attendants from his side, the trees by his side— resembling Varuṇa, the wielder of the noose—
seemed to utter the names of the intoxicated birds with the cries of the fowls.

And young creepers, impelled by the Maruts, scattered flowers over him— who resembled a friend of the Maruts and was worthy of worship— as he approached from nearby, like the daughters of the citizens scattering parched grain in accordance with custom.

Even though he was a wielder of the bow, the deer-eyed women, their hearts free from suspicion, perceived his compassionate nature; as they gazed upon his form, their eyes attained the full fruit of their great expansion.
In the groves, he heard his own fame being loudly sung by the forest deities, while the bamboos, their hollows filled with the wind, produced the effect of a flute as they whistled.
The breeze, mingled with the spray of forest waterfalls and fragrant with the scent of blossoms shaken from the trees,
attended upon him— who was purified by his conduct, who lacked a parasol, and who was weary from the heat of the sun.
Even without rain, the forest fire was extinguished; there was an extraordinary increase in fruits and flowers;
and while he entered that forest as its protector, no one among the creatures was oppressed by another.
Having purified the quarters of the sky with its wandering, at the close of day,
the radiance of the sun— copper-red like the hue of a young sprout— and the sage’s cow both set out to return to their respective abodes.
The protector of the middle world followed her for the sake of performing rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests;
accompanied by him, who was esteemed by the virtuous, she became like Faith herself visibly present through the performance of the prescribed ritual.

He proceeded, beholding forests turning dark green, where herds of boars had emerged from the ponds, where peacocks looked up toward the trees that served as their dwellings, and where the young grass was inhabited by deer.
The young cow, from the effort of bearing the weight of her full udders, and the lord of men, from the heaviness of his chest—
both adorned the path on their return from the penance grove with their graceful gaits.
As he was returning from the edge of the forest following Vasiṣṭha’s cow, his wife drank him in with her eyes,
the lashes of which were slow to blink, as if they had been fasting.
Honored on the path by the king and welcomed by the king’s lawful wife,
that cow shone between them like the twilight between day and night.
Having circumambulated that milch-cow, Sudakṣiṇā, with a vessel of parched grain in her hand,
bowed and worshipped its broad space between the horns as if it were the gateway to her own spiritual perfection.

Though anxious for her calf, she accepted the worship with composure; thus the two of them rejoiced, for in those endowed with devotion, the signs of grace from such beings are indeed the precursors of the fruit.
Having pressed the feet of his preceptor and his wife and completed the evening rites, Dilīpa—
having destroyed his enemies with his own arms— again attended upon the milch-cow as she sat down after the conclusion of her milking.

Having attended to her as she sat by the offerings and lamps placed nearby, the protector, accompanied by his wife, lay down after she had gradually fallen asleep; and when she rose at dawn, he rose after her.
Thus, as he of exalted fame— who was ever fit for uprooting his enemies— observed this vow for the sake of his subjects together with his queen,
seven times three days passed away.
On another day, the sage’s sacrificial cow, wishing to ascertain the disposition of her follower,
entered a cave of the Mountain of Gauri where young grass grew at the edge of the fall of the Ganges.

It is said that a lion, whose gaze was fixed upon the beauty of the mountain, suddenly seized her by force; for she was unassailable even in thought by predatory beasts, and the king did not notice his springing forward.

The king’s gaze, which the lord of mountains had granted him as if drawing it back by its rays, was turned away by that cry of distress from the afflicted sage, which was prolonged by its echo within the cave.
The archer beheld the lion standing upon the pale-red cow,
like a blossoming *rodhra* tree on the mineral-rich plateau of a mountain.

Then the king, who moved like the lord of beasts, who was a refuge for the distressed, and who had forcibly uprooted his enemies,— his anger aroused at the sight of the beast to be slain— desired to draw an arrow from his quiver for the sake of its slaughter.

The other hand of that archer, with its fingers still clinging to the feathered end of the arrow— its heron-feathers stained by the luster of his fingernails— remained as if its action were fixed in a painting.
His anger increased by the paralysis of his arms as he could not touch the offender standing nearby,
the king burned within himself with his own vital energy, like a serpent whose power is restrained by a mantra.

Having restrained his cow, the lion— whose lineage was noble and who was the banner of Manu’s race— addressed that king, a lion among men, in human speech, causing him wonder at his own supernatural power.
Enough of this exertion, O protector of the earth; even a weapon discharged against him would be in vain.
The force of the wind, though capable of uprooting trees, falters before a mountain.

Know me to be the servant named Kumbhodara, a friend of Nikumbha, whose back has been purified by the grace of the Lord of Eight Forms as He, desiring to mount His bull white as Mount Kailāsa, placed His footstep there.
Do you see yonder Devadāru tree before you? This tree was adopted as a son by the one whose banner bears the bull;
it is the one that knows the taste of the milk flowing from the golden-pitcher breasts of Skanda’s mother.
Once, while scratching his flank, the skin of this [elephant] was torn away by a wild elephant;
then the daughter of the Mountain grieved for him, as if for the commander of the celestial army pierced by the weapons of the Asuras.

From that time forth, the wielder of the trident, having assumed the form of a lion whose livelihood consists of preying upon creatures that come into his clutches, appointed me to this mountain cave for the purpose of terrifying elephants.
This [offering], ordained by the Supreme Lord for its time, is sufficient to satisfy this hungry one;
it has arrived as my feast of blood, just as the nectar of the moon is for the enemy of the gods.
Therefore, casting aside shame, you should return; for you have demonstrated devotion to your preceptor.
That which is to be protected by a weapon cannot be saved if it is impossible to do so; such a failure does not diminish the reputation of those who bear arms.
Having heard these bold words of the king of beasts, the sovereign of men,
his weapons rendered ineffectual by the power of Śiva, relaxed the self-contempt he had felt within himself.
And he replied to him regarding the discharge of the arrow during that first encounter,
his effort rendered futile by the gaze of Tryambaka, like the wielder of the thunderbolt wishing to release his vajra while paralyzed by the look of the Three-Eyed God.
"O Lord of Beasts, the words I wish to speak may well seem laughable to one whose movements are restrained;
yet you know every internal state of living beings, and therefore I shall speak."
He is venerable to me as the cause of the creation, preservation, and dissolution of all things moving and stationary;
and this wealth of my preceptor, who maintains the sacred fires, must not be neglected while it is perishing before our eyes.
Therefore, be gracious enough to sustain my bodily existence with your own body;
O Great Sage, let this cow, who is anxious for her calf at the close of day, be released.

Then, shattering the darkness of the mountain caves with the rays from his fangs, that attendant of the Lord of Beings laughed slightly and spoke again to Arthapati: *athāndhakāraṃ girikandarāṇāṃ daṃṣṭrāmayūkhaiḥ śakalāni kurvan / bhūyaḥ sa bhūteśvarapārśvavartī kiñcidvihasyārthapatiṃ babhāṣe //* Ragh(K)_2.46 //
Possessing sole sovereignty over the world under one umbrella, endowed with fresh youth and this lovely body,
you appear to me to be deluded by your lack of discernment in wishing to sacrifice so much for the sake of a trifle.
If this compassion for living beings is truly yours, then at the end of your life, let this single cow be safe;
for as long as you live, O Lord of Subjects, you shall protect your people from calamities like a father.
Now, you fear the punishment for the offense of a single cow from your preceptor, who is like a mere plowman;
yet his wrath can be appeased by you by touching him with cows by the millions, each with udders as large as jars.
Therefore, protect your own vigorous body, which is the enjoyer of a succession of auspicious fortunes;
for they say that a prosperous kingdom, distinct only by its contact with the surface of the earth, is the very station of Indra.

When the king of beasts had ceased speaking after saying this much, the mountain itself, through the echo returning from its caves, seemed to address that very same matter loudly to the protector of the earth with affection.
To the celestial attendant who had spoken such capable words, Dilīpa replied,
looking even more deeply moved by compassion as he was gazed upon by the cow, whose eyes were timid at the thought of his sitting upon her.
The exalted word "kṣatra" is indeed well-established in the worlds as meaning "one who protects from injury.
Of what use is a kingdom, or life itself, stained by infamy, to one whose conduct is the opposite of that?
And how could the great seer’s favor be won by the gift of other milch cows?
Know this: she is no less than Surabhi herself; you have struck her down through the power of Rudra.
Therefore, it is right for me to release you from him by paying the ransom of my own body;
in this way, your breaking of the fast will not be frustrated, and the purpose of the Sage’s ritual act will remain unimpaired.
Your Honor also understands this from the words of others, for great indeed is your effort toward the Devadāru tree;
yet it is possible for a protector to stand before his charge and destroy what must be protected himself, remaining unhurt.
If you consider me someone who must not be harmed, then be compassionate toward my body of fame;
for those like me truly have no attachment to material bodies that perish utterly.
They say that friendship is preceded by conversation; that bond was born between us when we met at the edge of the forest.
Therefore, O follower of the Lord of Beings, you ought not to reject the request of one who is your kinsman.
Saying "So be it" to the cow, Dilīpa immediately released his arm from its paralysis;
having laid down his weapons, he offered his own body to Hari as if it were a morsel of meat.
At that moment, as the protector of his subjects beheld the fierce descent of the lion,
a rain of flowers released from the hands of the Vidyādharas fell upon him as he hung with his face turned downward.
Having heard these words, which were like nectar, "Arise, my child," he rose up;
and having risen, the king saw before him his own cow, dripping with milk as if she were his mother, and not the lion.
To him who was thus amazed, the cow said: "O virtuous one, you have been tested by me through the manifestation of an illusion.
By the power of the sage, even Death himself is not able to strike me, much less other predators."
"O son, I am pleased with you because of your devotion to your guru and your compassion for me; choose a boon.
Know that I, the wish-fulfilling cow, being well-disposed, am not merely the source of milk."
Then, having summoned him, that king— who honored his supplicants and had earned for himself the title of "Hero" by his own hand—
begged for a son of infinite fame from Sudakṣiṇā, one who would be the founder of his lineage.
Having promised the king, who desired progeny, "So be it" to his wish, that milch-cow milked her own milk into a leaf-cup and instructed him, "My son, consume this."
O Mother, having obtained the sage’s permission for the remainder of the calf after the rules for the fire-oblation have been fulfilled,
I wish to enjoy your udder-milk, just as one enjoys the sixth part of the earth when it has been protected.
Thus addressed by the lord of the earth, Vasiṣṭha’s cow became even more pleased;
accompanied by him, she returned from the Himalayan slopes to the hermitage as if without any fatigue.

Having communicated his favor to his preceptor— the preceptor of kings— he whose face was like the bright moon declared it to his beloved once more with words that were a mere repetition, as her own cheerful countenance had already revealed it.

Having received permission from Vasiṣṭha, that man of blameless soul, who was ever affectionate toward his subjects, drank the milk of Nandinī— the remainder of what had been drunk by her calf— as if he were insatiable for pure fame once more.
At dawn, at the conclusion of the breaking of the fast as prescribed by his vow,
the self-controlled Vasiṣṭha performed the auspicious rite for departure and sent the royal couple back toward their own capital.
Having circumambulated the sacrificial fire into which oblations had been offered, and then his husband, Arundhatī,
and the cow with her calf, the king set forth, his majesty further intensified by these auspicious omens.
Accompanied by his lawful wife, the patient king traveled along a road pleasant for its lack of jolting, with a chariot whose sound was pleasing to the ear,
as if with his own fulfilled desire.
The subjects, distressed by his absence and their bodies emaciated by vows for the sake of progeny,
drank him in with eyes that found no satiety— him who was like the newly risen lord of medicinal herbs, filled with longing.
Having entered the city, which was adorned with raised banners, Purandaraśrī— being hailed by the citizens—
once again took up the burden of the earth upon his arm, which possessed strength equal to that of the king of serpents.
Then, as the sky receives the light arising from the eyes of Atri, or as the celestial river receives the splendor of Śiva cast forth by fire,
the queen conceived a fetus for the prosperity of the royal lineage— a fetus infused with the weighty majesty of the world-protectors.
Thus ends the second canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.

Then Sudakṣiṇā bore the signs of pregnancy— the very cause for the continuity of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the harbinger of her husband’s desired fulfillment, and the moonlight-like beginning of the glances of her circle of female friends.
With her face as pale as a ketaka petal, her slender body, and her few ornaments, she,
with her delicate form, imitated the night at dawn when the moon’s orb has grown faint and only a few stars remain.
Having smelled that face, which bore the scent of earth, the king did not reach satiety,
just as an elephant, at the end of the hot season, is never sated by a forest pond sprinkled with droplets from rain clouds.
"For my son shall enjoy the earth as Indra enjoys heaven, for his chariot shall rest only at the ends of the quarters;
therefore, she first fixed her mind upon such a desire, bypassing all other pleasures."
"Out of modesty, the Magadhan princess does not say anything of her desires; she merely yearns for certain things.
Thus did the Lord of Uttarakosala, full of respect, repeatedly question his beloved's female companions.
Having approached her state of longing and distress, whatever she chose was brought and seen by her;
for there was nothing desired by this king—even in the third heaven—that was difficult to obtain when his bow was strung.
As the days passed, her two breasts, pale as madhūka flowers with dark nipples,
bore the luster of ivory caskets covered with black antelope skins.
Having gradually overcome the discomfort of her pregnancy longings, she shone with the full development of her limbs, like a creeper that,
immediately upon the falling away of its old leaves, is adorned with beautiful new shoots.

The king regarded his queen as pregnant, like the ocean-clad earth containing hidden treasures, like a *śamī* tree with fire latent within, and like the Sarasvatī river with its waters flowing inside.

That steadfast king performed, in due order, the rites beginning with *puṃsavana*— rites appropriate to his love for his beloved, the exaltation of his mind, the wealth acquired by his arms from the ends of the earth, and his own fortitude.

The king rejoiced when she, having come to his house, rose from her seat with effort due to the weight of the womb resting upon Surendramātā, and greeted him with hands weary from the gesture of respectful salutation and eyes tremulous with emotion.
Then, attended by skilled physicians and trusted pediatricians within the maternity chamber, she stood ready for a safe delivery, shining like a ritual action whose fruit is imminent.

Then, at the auspicious time, Trishāḍhanā, who was like Śacī, gave birth to a son whose abundant fortune was indicated by five planets situated in their exaltations and not conjoined with the Sun, just as the power of the three means (tri-sādhana) produces unimpaired wealth.
The quarters became serene, the winds blew auspiciously, and the sacrificial fire accepted the oblation with its flames turning to the right;
at that moment, everything portended good fortune, for such an event as this leads to the prosperity of the world.
By the innate splendor of that noble-born one, which spread far and wide around his deathbed,
the midnight lamps were suddenly robbed of their luster and became as if fixed in a painting.

To the person of the inner apartments who announced the birth of the prince in words as sweet as nectar, there were only three things that the king could not give: the moon-bright parasol and the two fly-whisks.
Having at last beheld his son’s face, like a destitute man seeing a jar of buried treasure,
the father was so overcome with joy that he could no longer contain himself within his body, just as the ocean swells upon the rising of the moon.
When the entire birth-rite had been performed by the ascetic family priest who had come from the penance grove,
the son of Dilīpa shone all the more, like a gem risen from its mine that has undergone the proper refinement.
The sounds of auspicious musical instruments, pleasant to hear, accompanied by the joyful dances of courtesans,
resounded not only within the palace of the Lord of Magadha, but also along the path of the gods.
The protector did not fail to restrain anyone whom he might have liberated, being delighted by the birth of his son;
rather, at that time, he himself was alone released from the bondage of the ancestors known as the "debt."
Considering that this child would reach the end of what has been heard— that is, the Vedas— and likewise the end of others in battle, the king,
who understood the meaning of words, gave his own offspring the name Raghu, based on the root *ragh*, which signifies "going."
Through his father’s efforts and the fulfillment of all prosperity, he grew day by day with auspicious limbs,
like the young moon waxing through the entry of the rays of the sun.
Just as Umā and the Bull-bannered Lord rejoiced with Śarajanman, and Śacī and Purandara with Jayanta,
so too did the King and the Magadhan queen rejoice with their son, who was their equal and resembled them.

The mutual bond of affection between the two, who were like the two wheels of a chariot, did not diminish even though it was divided between their single son; rather, it remained directed toward one another.
When that child spoke his first words as prompted by his nurse, and when he walked while grasping her finger,
and when he became humble through the instruction of prostration— he thereby spread great joy for his father.
Placing him upon his lap, as if drenching his skin with the nectar born of physical contact,
the king, with his eyes half-closed, finally attained the experience of the taste of his son’s touch.
And the protector of the earth considered his own lineage, which was steadfast, to have attained its highest excellence through this son of noble birth;
just as the Lord of Creatures considers his own creation to be perfected by means of a distinct manifestation of himself characterized by the preeminent qualities.
With his topknot trimmed and accompanied by sons of ministers of his own age who wore dangling side-locks of hair,
he entered the ocean of literature through the mastery of writing, as one enters the sea by way of a river mouth.
Then the wise teachers duly instructed him, who had been initiated according to rule and was dear to his preceptor;
their efforts there were not in vain, for an action directed toward a worthy object bears fruit.
With his intellect noble and endowed with all virtues, he gradually crossed over the four branches of learning— which were like the four oceans—
just as the Lord of the Tawny-hued (the Sun) traverses the quarters of the sky with his bay horses that outspeed the wind.
Having donned the sacred skin of the ruru deer, he practiced the science of weapons from his father himself according to the mantras;
he became the foremost knower of the secrets of the discharge and withdrawal of weapons, just like Purandara.
Like a young calf attaining the state of a great bull, or like a young elephant reaching the condition of a lordly tusker,
Raghu— his childhood gradually supplanted by youth— cultivated a body that was both profound and enchanting.
Then, immediately after the ceremony of the tonsure (godāna), the Lord performed the initiation for marriage;
having obtained that virtuous husband, the daughters of the king shone like the daughters of Dakṣa who had gained the Sun, the dispeller of darkness.

A youth with arms as long as a yoke, muscular, with a chest like a door-panel and a thick-set neck, Raghu surpassed his elder by the excellence of his physique; nevertheless, he appeared humble through his modesty.

Then, perceiving through the eye of his intellect that his son was self-controlled, the king— intending to lighten the exceedingly heavy burden of subjects which he himself had long borne— made his son the bearer of the title "Crown Prince."

Then Fortune, desiring his virtues, departed from the primary abode of the king— the one known as the crown prince— and went to that residence with a portion of herself, like a lotus moving from its source to a newly blossomed flower.
Like the sun at dawn with the wind as its charioteer, or like the sun with its rays after the departure of the clouds,
that king became exceedingly difficult to withstand because of him, just as an elephant becomes so through the bursting of its temples.
Having appointed him to guard the sacrificial horse, followed by princes who were archers, he—
resembling Indra— completed a hundred sacrifices without obstacle, lacking only one.
After this,

Śakra, it is said, having assumed a concealed form, seized the horse that had been released without restraint for the sacrifice by that sacrificer, even in the very presence of the archers who were its guards.
Then the prince’s army stood still, struck with wonder and its resolve lost in despondency;
at that moment, Nandinī, the cow of Vasiṣṭha, whose power was renowned, appeared there by chance.

Then, having wiped his eyes with a meritorious drop of the fluid flowing from his limbs, the son of Dilīpa became one for whom vision was attained even regarding objects beyond the senses, as he was held in high esteem by the virtuous.
Born from a king of men, he beheld to the east the god who shatters the wings of mountains;
repeatedly restrained by the charioteer from his restlessness, the god was carrying away the horse that was tethered to the chariot by its reins.
Recognizing Hari by his hundreds of unblinking eyes and by his tawny horses,
Raghu addressed him in a deep voice that touched the heavens, as if calling him back.
O Lord of the Gods, since you alone are declared by the wise to be the foremost among those who partake in the sacrificial portions,
how can you proceed to obstruct the ritual of my preceptor, who is engaged in perpetual consecration?
As the Lord of the three worlds, you who possess divine vision must surely restrain the enemies of sacrifice;
yet if you yourself, though practicing dharma, become an obstacle to their rites, then the sacred law has been subverted.
Therefore, O Maghavan, you ought to release this horse, the foremost limb of the great sacrifice;
for lords who show the pure path do not adopt a defiled track.
Having heard these bold words uttered by Raghu, the lord of the gods,
filled with wonder, turned his chariot back and proceeded to offer a reply.
O Prince, it is as you have said; glory must indeed be protected on all sides by those for whom glory is their wealth.
Yet your father is prepared to transgress that entire world-renowned path through his sacrificial rites.
Just as Hari alone is remembered as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), and Maheśvara, the Three-eyed One, alone and no other;
so do the sages know me, O performer of a hundred sacrifices, for this title of ours does not apply to a second person.
Therefore, this horse was carried off by me from your father while he was imitating Kapila;
enough of this effort on your part—do not set foot upon the path of Sagara’s progeny.
Then, free from fear, the son of the Indra of the earth laughed and spoke again to Purandara:
"Take up your weapon if this is your resolve; indeed, you shall not achieve your purpose without first conquering Raghu."
Having spoken thus to Maghavan, he stood with his face upturned, about to string his bow with an arrow,
emulating the Lord [Śiva] with a physical excellence graced by the distinguished *ālīḍha* posture.
Wounded in the heart by Raghu’s arrow— which was composed of sheer audacity— even the indignant Indra,
the breaker of mountains, fixed an unerring shaft upon his bow, which bore the momentary mark of a fresh bank of clouds.
Having entered the broad chest of the prince, that swift arrow— already accustomed to the blood of terrible demons—
fell upon human blood as if out of curiosity, for it had never tasted such before.

The prince of Hari, possessing the prowess of a youth, also fixed an arrow marked with his own name upon the arm of Indra— the arm that was calloused by the lashing of the celestial elephant’s trunk and adorned with the decorative leaf-patterns of Śacī.
And with another arrow marked by a peacock feather, he struck down Indra’s great thunderbolt-bannered standard;
the king of the gods grew violently incensed at him, as if his very hair had been forcibly shorn away from the goddess Śrī.

A tumultuous battle took place between those two seekers of victory, with their armies of Siddhas stationed nearby, as they struck with feathered arrows— some facing downward and others facing upward— that were as terrifying to behold as Garuḍas and venomous serpents.
Vāsava was unable to extinguish that abode of unbearable splendor with showers of weapons discharged in continuous succession,
just as a cloud cannot extinguish with its waters a fire that has fallen from itself.

Then, with an arrow whose head was shaped like the crescent moon, Raghu severed the bowstring of Indra from his forearm, which was marked with yellow sandalwood paste, as it resounded deeply like the churning ocean.

Casting aside his bow, his envy further inflamed, he took up a weapon that was radiant with a shimmering halo— raised for the purpose of banishing his powerful enemy and resembling the destruction of the wings of the mountains.
Struck violently in the chest by him, Raghu fell to the ground along with the tears of his soldiers;
yet, having shaken off the pain in a mere moment, he rose up together with the shouts of joy from the troops.

Nevertheless, as he remained steadfast even while his enemies persisted in their hostile attitude, cruel in their use of weapons, the slayer of Vṛtra was gratified by his extraordinary valor; for a position is established everywhere through virtues alone.
"Even among the mountains, my weapon has never been withstood by anyone other than you because of its inherent power;
know that I am pleased, and choose a boon, with the exception of the horse," said the slayer of Vṛtra to him.
Then, withdrawing the arrow— which had been drawn from the quiver but not fully released, its golden shafts coloring his fingers— the son of Dilīpa, speaking kindly, replied to the Lord of the Gods.
If my lord deems it right that the horse not be released, then, once the ritual is completed according to the prescribed rules,
may my preceptor— whose body has been consecrated by continuous initiation— be endowed today with the full fruit of the sacrifice.
O Lord of Heaven, since you are a portion of the Three-eyed One (Śiva) and thus difficult to approach,
please ensure that the lord of the people hears this account from the messenger of your very own message while he is seated in the assembly hall.
Saying "So be it," Mātali, whose charioteership was his skill, accepted Rāghava’s request and departed as he had come;
the son of Sudakṣiṇā also returned to the king’s assembly hall, his heart not yet fully at ease.
The Lord of Creatures, awakened first by the messenger of Hari’s command,
greeted him while stroking his body— marked with the scars of the thunderbolt— with a hand trembling with joy.
Thus the lord of the earth, whose commands were honored, having performed ninety-nine great sacrifices,
as his life drew to a close, ascended toward heaven as if constructing a flight of stairs.

Then he, with his mind withdrawn from the objects of the senses, having according to the prescribed rite bestowed the white sunshade—the insignia of sovereignty—upon his young son, took refuge in the shade of a tree in a sage’s grove together with that queen; for this is the family vow of the Ikṣvākus when their age has declined.
Thus ends the third canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.
Having accepted the kingdom bestowed by his father, he shone even more brightly,
like the sacrificial fire when the radiance deposited at the end of the day returns to the sun.
And for those kings who heard that Dilīpa had laid down his weapons and that he was their sovereign,
it was as if a spear had been driven into their hearts from which all other arrows had been extracted.
Like the rows of banners on Indra’s standard,
the subjects, together with their children, rejoiced at the sight of his new accession to power.
Simultaneously, he who moved with the gait of an elephant ascended both his father’s lion-throne and the entire circle of his enemies.
It is said that Padmā herself, remaining invisible, attended upon him who was consecrated for imperial sovereignty, using her own shadow as the target for her lotus-umbrella.
And whenever the bards approached at the proper times,
Sarasvatī, appearing as if personified, attended upon him who was worthy of praise with hymns of meaningful laudation.
Although the earth had been enjoyed by honorable kings beginning with Manu, nevertheless, it was as if it had never belonged to anyone else before him.
For, by administering just punishment, he won the hearts of the entire world,
like the southern breeze which is neither too cold nor too hot.
Granted that her eyes resembled the petals of a lotus,
yet true sight comes through the scripture, which reveals the meaning of subtle matters.
Just as the moon is so called because it gladdens, and the sun because it heats,
even so did that king become true to his name by pleasing his subjects.
Those skilled in statecraft presented both the right and the wrong courses to the new king;
yet only the former position prevailed with him, while the latter did not.

Because of his superior virtues toward his elder, the subjects were made to feel diminished longing for him, just as people feel less anticipation for the blossoming of a mango tree when its fruit is already present.
The qualities of all five elements flourished in their excellence under that new protector of the earth; everything seemed as if it were new again.
Then, royal fortune— characterized by autumnal lotuses— approached him who was established in well-being through the pacification [of his senses] he had attained, like a second Śarad herself.
With the clouds having shed their rain and become light, the quarters of the sky expanded for both him and the sun, as if they had been cleared away to make room for their increasing brilliance.
Thinking, "This is the time for Raghu to string his weapon," Indra,
as if apprehensive, withdrew his own bow.
The season, with its white lotuses as parasols and its blooming kāśa flowers as fly-whisks, imitated him; yet it did not attain his splendor.
Then, as that king was gracious and pleasant of countenance and the moon possessed a clear radiance,
the delight of those with eyes was equal toward both.
Upon the rows of swans, upon the stars, and upon the waters filled with white lotuses,
the glories of his kinsmen seemed to have been scattered like his own fame.
Seated in the shade of sugarcanes, the women guarding the rice fields sang of the fame of that protector,
extolling his rising virtues from the time of his childhood onwards.
The waters became clear at the rising of the great-spirited Kumbhayoni (Agastya),
but the minds of his enemies, fearing the defeat of Raghu, were agitated.
Mighty bulls, fierce with rut, humped, and tearing up the banks of rivers,
encountered his prowess with playful ease.
Struck by the blossoms of the *saptaparṇa* trees, which were fragrant with rut-fluid,
those elephants exuded [ichor] from seven parts of their bodies as if out of indignation.
Making the rivers fordable and the roads free of thick mud,
the autumn season first urged him toward his expedition by means of its favorable power.
To him, the fire, properly fed with oblations during the rite of the "Victory-illumination" (vājinīrājanā),
bestowed victory as if with a hand, under the guise of its flames turning to the right.
With his frontiers and rear-guard protected, his flanks pure,
and endowed with speed, he set forth with his sixfold army, desiring to conquer the quarters.
The city women, advanced in years, scattered parched grain over him,
just as the waves of the milk-ocean, tossed by Mount Mandara, showered droplets upon Acyuta.
Equal to Prācīnabarhis, he first went toward the east,
as if threatening with his banners tossed by the wind like snakes that had been provoked.
Making the sky appear like the surface of the earth with the dust raised by his chariots, and the surface of the earth appear like the sky with his elephants resembling massive clouds; Ragh(K) 4.29.
First came his majesty, then the sound of his chariot, followed by the vanguard;
and finally the elephant division marched behind—it was as if that army were moving in four distinct columns.
The rivers along his path were made turbid by those who preceded him, shallow by those who traveled with him, and muddy by those who followed behind.
By virtue of his power, he made the mountain ridges abound with water, the navigable rivers easy to cross, and the forests illuminated.
Leading that great army toward the eastern ocean,
he shone like Bhagīratha leading the Gaṅgā as it falls from the matted locks of Śiva.
With kings deprived of their fruits, uprooted, and broken in many ways,
his path was made prominent by them, just as that of an elephant by trees.
Thus traversing those various eastern regions one after another,
he reached the shore of the great ocean, dark with groves of palm trees.
Therefore, from that uprooter of the unsubmissive, as if from the current of a river,
the Suhmas protected themselves by adopting the behavior of a reed.
Having swiftly uprooted the Vaṅgas who were arrogant in their naval forces,
that leader planted pillars of victory within the channels of the Ganges' current.
Bowing down as far as their lotus-feet like rice stalks,
they, having been uprooted and replanted, caused Raghu to flourish with their fruits.
Having crossed the Kāverī with his troops by means of a bridge of bound elephants,
he proceeded toward Kaliṅga, his path being shown by the people of Utkala.
He fixed his sharp prowess upon the head of Mahendra,
just as a driver fixes a goad upon the head of a deep-sensing elephant.
The King of Kaliṅga, whose force was his elephants, countered him with missiles,
just as a mountain raining down stones opposes Indra when he is intent on clipping its wings.
Having endured there the storm of iron arrows from his enemies, the descendant of Kakutstha attained the glory of victory as if he had bathed in an auspicious rite.
Like Garuda seizing a serpent from the ocean, he seized the King of Kaliṅga from the elephant division, which had been shaken off by the Vāyavya weapon as if it were a mass of wings.
Having prepared their drinking grounds with the leaves of betel vines,
his warriors drank coconut liquor as well as the fame of their enemies.
That king, victorious through righteousness, having captured and then released [the enemy],
took away the modesty of the lord of Mahendra, but not his land.
Then, along the very shore of the sea, which was garlanded with rows of fruit-bearing betel-nut trees,
he proceeded toward the quarter frequented by Agastya, desiring victory that could not be doubted.
By the enjoyment of his army, fragrant with the ichor of elephants,
he made the Kāverī river seem as if it were a rival to the lord of rivers, the ocean.
By him, the dust of the army was made to serve as a substitute for cosmetic powder upon the tresses of the Kerala women, who had cast off their ornaments out of fear.
The foothills of the Malaya mountain, where black pepper was left behind by the harīta birds, were occupied by the forces of that king who had set out on his campaign of conquest.
The dust, arising from the fields of ripening paddy trampled by the hooves of well-bred horses,
suddenly pervaded the sky, which was already turbid with the cocoons of silkworms.

The neck-chains of the elephants, though they tore through their foot-tethers, did not slip off even as they moved along the paths encircled by the coils of serpents, for they were fastened with sandalwood.
In that very southern quarter, even the splendor of the sun grows dim;
therein the Pāṇḍyas could not endure the majesty of Raghu.
Having descended, they presented to him the finest pearls from the great ocean joined by the Tāmraparṇī river,
as if offering their own accumulated glory.
Having enjoyed himself at will upon those two mountains, Malaya and Dardura, which had sandalwood trees growing freely upon their slopes, he rested like the two breasts of that southern quarter.
He of irresistible prowess crossed the Sahya mountain, which had been left far behind by the ocean,
like the slope of the earth with its garment of clouds slipping away.
By his advancing armies, intent on conquering the western regions,
even though he was driven back from Rāma, he remained as if clinging to the Sahya mountains like the ocean.
The ketaka pollen, stirred up by the wind ahead of him,
became the effortless fragrant powder for the turbans of his warriors.
The rustling sound of his horses and chariots was surpassed by the whistling of the groves of royal palm trees shaken by the wind.
From the *punnāga* trees, bees fell upon the temples of the elephants— temples bound with the trunks of date palms and fragrant with the exudation of rut.
Requested by Rāma, the Ocean indeed granted him space;
under the pretext of being the king of the western frontier, he paid tribute to the descendant of Raghu.
There, he made Mount Trikūṭa itself a lofty pillar of victory, upon which were carved distinct marks of his prowess by the tusks of his great elephants.
Then he set out by a land route to conquer the Persians,
just as a self-controlled ascetic sets out with the knowledge of reality to conquer the enemies known as the senses.
He could not endure the intoxication of the wine from the lotus-faces of the Yavana women,
just as the unseasonable rising of clouds cannot endure the morning sun for the lotuses.
A tumultuous battle took place with him against the cavalry of the Persians;
in the dust, the opposing combatants could only be identified by the twanging of their Śārṅga bows.
With their bearded heads severed by his arrows,
he covered the earth as if with honeycombs swarming with bees.
The remaining ones, having removed their helmets, sought refuge with him;
for the indignation of great-souled men is appeased by prostration.
On the vine-covered grounds where precious deer-skins were spread, those warriors dispelled the fatigue of their victory with honeyed drinks.
Then Raghu set out toward the northern quarter like the sun,
intending to extract the wealth of the northerners with his arrows as the sun draws up moisture with its rays.
Having made those very conquerors his precursors on the chariots,
the unconquerable one entered the Northern Region like the submarine fire entering the great ocean.
Having their fatigue on the road dispelled by the twisting around the banks of the Vaṅkṣu,
his horses shook their saddles, from which the filaments of saffron were clinging.
There, the exploits of Raghu against the husbands of the Hun women displayed his manifest prowess, serving as an instruction for the laceration of their cheeks.
The Kambojas were unable to withstand his prowess in battle;
they were forced to bow down along with the akṣoṭa trees that had been strained by being used as elephant-tethers.
Masses of wealth, consisting mostly of excellent horses and towering in height,
entered that lord of the people like rivers flowing into the ocean.
Then, accompanied by his retinue, he ascended the mountain, the father of Gaurī,
as if increasing its peaks with the rising dust of minerals.
He praised those of equal courage who remained unperturbed even amidst the roar of the army,
like lions dwelling in caves who turn their heads to look back.
On the way, the breezes— making the birch leaves rustle and causing the whistling sound of the hollow bamboos— served him with sprays from the Ganges.
The soldiers took rest,
sitting upon rocks whose surfaces were scented by the musk of deer reclining there, beneath the shade of *nameru* trees.
At night, the nearby medicinal herbs, their brilliance enhanced by the neck-chains of elephants tethered to the *sarala* trees,
served as oil-less lamps for the leader.
In his dwellings, the deodar trees, through their friction against the temples of elephants moistened by rut-fluid as they rubbed them together,
revealed to the Kirātas that he possessed the stature of a great elephant.
There, a fierce conflict took place with those mountaineers,
in which fire burst forth from the impact of iron arrows, slings, and stones.
Having made the Utsavasanketas pay tribute with his arrows,
that successful king caused the Kinnaras to sing the praises of the victory of his arms.
As they stood before one another with offerings in their hands,
the King perceived the essence of the Himalayas, and the Himalayan mountain perceived the essence of the King.
There, having established Akṣobhya as a mass of glory, he descended [from the mountain],
as if taking away the shame of the mountain that had been rivalled by Rāvaṇa.
When he had crossed the Lauhitya river, the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa trembled along with the black aloe-wood trees that had served as the tethering posts for his elephants.
He could not even endure the dust raised by the rows of chariots— which obscured the sun and created a cloudy, gloomy day— let alone the enemy's army with its banners.
The Lord [of Laṅkā], whose prowess surpassed that of Indra, employed against him elephants with split temples— capable of assuming any form at will— which he had previously used to besiege others.
The Lord of Kāmarūpa worshipped the shadow of his feet— the presiding deity of the golden throne— with an offering of jewel-like flowers.
Thus, having conquered the quarters, the Victorious One returned, laying to rest the dust raised by his chariot upon the crests of kings whose umbrellas were now withdrawn.
He performed the Viśvajit sacrifice, in which his entire possessions were given as the sacrificial fee;
for the acquisitions of the virtuous are indeed for the sake of distribution, just like the gathering of clouds by rain-bearing winds.

At the conclusion of the sacrificial session, the descendant of Kakutstha, accompanied by his ministers, permitted the kings— whose grief over defeat had been assuaged by grand honors and whose queens were longing for their long-absent departure— to return to their own cities.
With prostrations at his departure, they made the pair of feet of the emperor— which bore the marks of the lines, the banner, the jar, and the parasol, and were obtainable through his grace—
yellowish-white with the pollen and nectar falling from the garlands on their crowns as they touched his toes.
Thus ends the fourth canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.
To that lord of the earth at the Viśvajit sacrifice, who had distributed his entire treasury in total generosity,
Kautsa— the disciple of Varatantu— approached, having acquired knowledge and seeking the means for his teacher’s fee.
Having placed the guest-offering (*arghya*) in an earthen vessel because he was devoid of golden ones, that king of most noble character—
illustrious for his fame and radiant with sacred learning— went out to meet the guest who was worthy of hospitality.

Having honored that ascetic according to the prescribed rites, the lord of the people— who was skilled in discerning what ought to be done, foremost among those whose wealth is honor, and proficient in ritual knowledge— spoke with palms joined in reverence to him who sat upon his seat.
O you of sharp intellect, is your preceptor well— he who was the foremost among the seers who composed mantras—
since from him you have obtained complete knowledge, just as one initiated [into a sacrifice] receives consciousness from the fierce [deity]?

I hope that the threefold austerity of the Great Seer— performed through body, speech, and mind— is not being thwarted by obstacles, nor is it causing a loss of fortitude in the Wielder of the Thunderbolt.

I trust that no calamity from wind or other elements has befallen the trees of your hermitage— which dispel fatigue and have been nurtivated with efforts beginning from the securing of their foundations— as if they were your own sons.

Out of affection, even for the sake of ritual requirements, the sages have not broken the desires [of the deer] regarding the *kuśa* grass; thus, I hope that the birth of the does remains unblemished, as their umbilical cords do not fall upon the beds where they rest in their laps.

I trust that the auspicious waters of the sacred fords are well with you— those waters whose sands are marked by the sixth part of gleaned grain, from which the ritual ablutions for the observances are performed and from which the handfuls of water-offerings for the ancestors are drawn.

I trust that the forest produce you obtain for the maintenance of your bodies— such as the ripening wild rice and other grains— is accepted by the country folk without resentment, and that it serves as the portion for guests who arrive at the proper time.
Has the great seer, being well-pleased, permitted you to return home after having properly instructed you?
For now is the time for you to proceed to the second stage of life, which is capable of providing all assistance.
My mind is not satiated by merely visiting you, the Arhat; it is eager to carry out your command.
Whether by the order of your teacher or of your own accord, you have come from the forest to honor me.

Having heard Raghu’s noble speech regarding the cow, though he had inferred Raghu’s immense wealth from the vessel for the guest-offering (arghya), Kautsa—his hopes for his own purpose now weakened—replied to him who was free from reproach: *ityarghyapātrānumitavyayasya raghorudārām api gāṃ niśamya / svārthopapattiṃ prati durbalāśaḥ pratyāha kautsastamapetakutsam //* Ragh(K) 5.12. “Thus, having heard Raghu’s noble words concerning the cow, even though Raghu’s expenditure had been inferred from the vessel for the guest-offering, Kautsa, his hope for the attainment of his own goal being weak, replied to that king who was devoid of reproach.”
"Know, O King, that all is well with us; for while you are our protector, how could misfortune befall your subjects?
When the sun is shining, how could darkness possibly serve as an obscuration to the vision of the world?"

Devotion toward those worthy of honor is appropriate for your lineage; by your great magnanimity, you have surpassed your ancestors. Yet, it is my sorrow that I have come to you as a petitioner only after the proper time has passed.
O Lord of Men, standing there with only your body, you shine with the splendor bestowed by sacred fords;
you resemble a stalk of wild rice remaining after the grain has been gathered by forest-dwellers, its fruit-bearing capacity exhausted.
It is fitting that you, being the sole lord of men, manifest this state of possessing nothing born of sacrifice;
for the waning of the digits of the moon after it has been drunk by the gods in succession is indeed more praiseworthy than its waxing.
Therefore, since I have no other duty, I shall strive to procure the teacher’s fee from elsewhere;
may it be well with you, for even the *cātaka* bird does not distress a cloud in autumn whose interior has shed its water.

Having said this much, the king restrained the disciple of the great seer who was desiring to depart, and questioned him: "O wise one, what object should be given by you to the teacher, and of what extent?"
Then that wise student related the matter at hand to him, the preceptor of the social orders and stages of life, who had duly performed the sacrifice and was free from the influence of pride.
Having acquired knowledge, I requested the great seer for the preceptor’s fee;
he, however, regarded my long-standing and unswerving devotion as being foremost.
Then, his anger aroused by my persistence, my teacher, disregarding my emaciated state, said to me:
"Bring me fourteen crores of wealth, according to the number of sciences you have mastered."

Therefore, perceiving you to be one whose title of "Lord" remains as a mere remnant, I venture now to detain you with this vessel for the rites of hospitality; for the price of my learning is no small matter.
Thus addressed by the twice-born, the best among those who know the Vedas,
he who possessed the splendor of the moon and whose sensory activities were turned away from sin, the sole lord of the world spoke further to him.

May this not become for me a fresh occasion of reproach: that one who was seeking wealth for his teacher, who had mastered the Vedas, yet failed to obtain his desire from Raghu, went to another donor.
O worthy one, you who have been honored by me, dwelling in my palace like the fourth sacred fire in the sacrificial chamber,
you ought to endure two or three days while that which is intended for your sake is being prepared.

Saying "So be it," the one of noble birth, Raghu, having understood his word to be infallible, accepted the challenge; and beholding the earth as one whose wealth had been taken away, he desired to extract that wealth from Kubera.
Due to the power born from the sprinkling of Vasiṣṭha’s mantras, the movement of his chariot was not obstructed even upon the ocean, the sky, or the mountains,
just like that of a cloud accompanied by the wind.

Then at nightfall, the steadfast Raghu, purified in his observances, lay down upon the chariot prepared for him with its interior filled with weapons; he did so out of a mere suspicion that his vassals might be plotting against him, desiring to conquer the Lord of Kailāsa by force.
In the morning, as he was preparing to depart, those appointed to observe him reported with astonishment that a rain of gold had fallen from the sky into the middle of the treasury.
The king bestowed that entire heap of radiant gold, which he had obtained from Kuvera as he was being assailed,
upon Kautsa— like a peak of Mount Sumeru shattered by the thunderbolt.
To the people dwelling in Sāketa, both of them were objects of veneration;
the petitioner was free from desire for more than what was due to his preceptor, while the king bestowed even more than what the petitioner desired.

Then, having obtained his wealth by means of a hundred female camels and mules, the wise Kautsa, with a joyful heart, touched the lord of subjects—who had bent his upper body forward—with his hand as he was about to depart, and spoke these words: *athoṣṭravāmīśatahāritārthaṃ prajeśvaraṃ prītamanā manīṣī / spṛśankareṇānatapūrvakāyaṃ samprasthito vākyamuvāca kautsaḥ //* Ragh(K)_5.32 // "Then, having acquired his riches through a hundred female camels and mares, the wise Kautsa, his mind filled with joy, touched the lord of the people—whose forebody was bowed low—with his hand, and as he set out, he addressed him with these words."
What wonder is there in this, that the earth yields all desires for you, the sovereign of subjects who abide in righteous conduct?
But your power is truly inconceivable, by which even the heavens were milked according to your wish.
For you who have attained all blessings, any other wish would be redundant; may you obtain a son worthy of your own virtues, who, like your venerable father, shall be an object of praise for you.
Having thus offered his benediction, the foremost of beings returned to the presence of his preceptor;
the king, for his part, quickly obtained a son from him, just as the world of living beings receives light from the sun.
It is said that during the *brāhma* hour, his queen gave birth to a son who was like Kumāra himself;
therefore, his father named that first-born son Aja after the name of Brahmā.
The prince possessed that same vigorous form, that same prowess, and that same natural loftiness;
he did not differ from his progenitor, just as a lamp lit from another lamp does not differ from it.

Though the Goddess of Fortune desired him— who had duly acquired learning from his gurus and was exceptionally handsome with the onset of youth— she waited for her father’s permission like a steadfast maiden awaiting her father’s consent.
Then King Aśvapati of the Krathakaiśikas, eager to bring his nephew to the svayaṃvara of his sister Indumatī,
dispatched a trusted messenger to Raghu with Bhoja.
Reflecting upon that praiseworthy alliance and considering his son to have reached the stage suitable for marriage,
he dispatched him with an army to the prosperous capital of the Lord of Vidarbha.

For the son of the lord of men, the halting-places along the road— wherein hospitality was prepared in the guest-houses and which were distinguished from others by the offerings of the local people— became like pleasure-gardens for recreation.

Having traversed the road, he encamped his army— whose horses from the forest of Āyodhyā were frothing with fatigue— on the bank of the Narmadā, where the rows of banners were made to dance by breezes moist with spray.
Then, preceded by bees hovering above that signaled his entry into the water,
a wild elephant emerged from the river, its broad temples washed clean of rut.
On the slopes of Ṛkṣavān,

he indicated the traces of his passage by means of his two tusks, which were blunted against the rocks and mottled with dark vertical streaks, as if they were the ridges of a mountain washed by the floodwaters.
With a hand capable of swift withdrawal and extension, he shone as he suddenly broke the waves facing the shore with a roar, like one who has begun to break through the bolts of a door with his arm.

Skilled in the waters, he drew along the mossy creepers clinging to the bank as he moved toward the shore, while the soft tendrils— left over from the *kāraṇḍava* ducks and serving as the waist-bands of the Pulinda women sporting in the water— were pulled away by him.
The splendor of the rutting-fluid, which had been momentarily stilled on the temples of that solitary elephant as he plunged into the lake,
blazed forth once again at the sight of other wild elephants.
Having smelled his unbearable rut, which flowed with the pungent milk of seven-leaved trees,
the lordly elephants of the army turned away, despite the strenuous efforts of their mahouts to restrain them.

In an instant, he threw that military camp into a tumultuous state: its yokes were severed and its draft animals fled, leaving it empty; its chariots had broken axles and were overturned; and its warriors were distracted by the need to rescue their women.

Hearing that the wild elephant was not to be slain by the king, the prince drew his Śārṅga bow neither too far nor too short and struck it on the forehead with an arrow as it charged toward him, intending to turn it back.
As soon as he was pierced, it is said that he cast off his serpent form while being watched by the astonished army,
and assumed a beautiful celestial body standing in the midst of a shimmering halo of light.
Then, having showered the prince with flowers produced from the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*) brought forth by his own power,
the eloquent king spoke, the pearl necklace upon his chest made to appear even more radiant by the luster of his teeth.
"Know me to be Priyamvada, the son of Priyadarshana, the lord of the Gandharvas; through the curse of Matanga, rooted in my own arrogance, I have attained the state of an elephant."
And after I had subsequently entreated that great seer with prostrations, he became gentle;
for while heat arises from contact with fire and sunlight, coolness is indeed the natural state of water.
"When Aja, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, shall break your jar with an iron-tipped arrow,
you will be reunited with your own majesty"— thus did that treasure of asceticism speak to me.
I have been liberated from the time of my curse by you and have attained the destiny ordained by the Creator;
for if I were not to perform a service for you in return, my recovery of my own status would indeed be in vain.
Therefore, accept from me this Gandharva weapon, whose mantras for its employment and withdrawal are distinct;
it is named Prasvāpana, by which the striker gains victory while causing no harm to his enemies.
Enough of this shame toward me, since for a moment you were intent on compassion even while striking me;
therefore, when I am being entreated, you should not employ the harshness of refusal.

Saying "So be it," that moon among men, the knower of weapons, sipped the purifying water of the river born from Soma while facing north; he then received from him the mantra for the weapon, having restrained his speech.
Thus, as they traveled along the road, a friendship arose between them through the power of fate, its cause beyond imagination;
one went toward the regions of Caitraratha, delightful due to their excellent governance, while the other went to Vidarbha.
As he stood near the outskirts of the city, the King of Krathakaiśika— filled with a profound joy born from the news of his arrival—
went out to meet him, like a surging ocean with its waves rising toward the moon.

Having led him into the city, the leader, whose glory was now humbled, attended upon him with such lowliness that all the people gathered there thought the Lord of Vidarbha had come to his own home as a guest.

Pointed out by his bowing attendants, that representative of Raghu ascended the beautiful new palace, where golden jars were placed at the eastern entrance; it was as if the God of Love had entered a stage of life beyond childhood.

There, sleep— clouded by the perception of his inner state— finally appeared before the eyes of Aja, who desired that lovely jewel of a maiden for whom the assembly of kings had gathered at her *svayaṃvara*, like a beloved woman appearing after a long time.

At dawn, bards awakened him—who resembled the rising sun—with voices charming through their graceful composition; he whose thick shoulders were pressed by his ear-ornaments and whose body-unguents were thinned by friction against the covers of his bed.
The night has passed, O best among the wise; leave your bed. Surely the burden of the world was divided into two parts by the Creator:
that which your father bears with unwearied effort on one side, and you, who support the position of his other successor, on the other.

Overcome by sleep and left unheeded by you at night, the Goddess Lakṣmī experiences longing like a woman whose lover has abandoned her; even the moon, hanging low on the edge of the horizon, loses its luster before the radiance of your face.
By that simultaneous and beautiful opening, let these two immediately attain mutual likeness:
your eye, with its pupil quivering and soft within, and the lotus, with its bee moving inside.
The morning breeze loosens the flowers from the stalks of the trees and mingles with the lotuses opened by the rays of the dawn;
it seems as if it seeks to acquire for itself the natural fragrance of your breath through the excellence of another.
The snowy water, fallen upon copper-hued tree shoots and as bright as polished pearl beads from a necklace,
appears as if it were your own smile— intermingled with the moonlight of your teeth and having acquired a heightened luster from contact with your bimba-red lips.
Before the sun, the treasury of heat, can suddenly assail [the world], darkness has already been dispelled by Aruṇa;
for when you, O hero, have taken the lead at the front of the battle, why should your preceptor himself destroy the enemies?
