Those army elephants, having shaken off sleep on both sides, leave their beds while dragging their clanging chains;
their tusks shine with the hue of the young sun, appearing like the slopes of a mountain split open and stained with red ochre.
O lotus-eyed one, these horses from Vanāyu, having shaken off their sleep while tethered in long cloth pavilions,
now blacken with the heat of their mouths the pieces of rock-salt placed before them to be licked.
Devotion has become sparse, the offerings of flowers have withered, and the lamps are devoid of the radiance of their surrounding halos;
even this sweet-voiced parrot of yours in its cage repeats our words intended to awaken you.
Thus, having shaken off his sleep, that broad-shouldered prince left his couch— like the elephant Supratīka leaving the sandy bank of the Ganges—
and released the edge of the bed-covering which had been bitten by the jewels of the bracelets of the women of his retinue as they were busy at his feet.
Then, having completed the rites prescribed by the scriptures appropriate for the beginning of the day, he— whose eyelashes were curved,
whose attire was skillfully fashioned to suit him, and who was adorned with ornaments— went to the assembly of kings gathered for the svayaṃvara.
Thus ends the fifth canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.
There he beheld kings seated upon thrones on couches resembling celestial palaces, their physical splendor intensified by their ornaments, like sacrificial posts erected upon golden altars.

As the kings gazed upon the descendant of Kakutstha— who, as it were, had his own body returned to him by the Lord through the mediation of Rati’s favor— their hearts became despondent regarding Indumatī.
Then the prince ascended the dais pointed out by Vaidarbha by means of a prepared flight of stairs,
just as a lion cub climbs a lofty mountain peak by means of its rocky ledges.
Seated upon a jewel-encrusted throne covered with a most excellent carpet,
he possessed a splendor that was almost rivaled by Guha, who rested upon the back of a peacock.

In those royal successions, resplendent with glory, he shone as his self divided a thousandfold— difficult to behold due to the emergence of such extraordinary radiance— just as lightning flashes through rows of clouds.
In the midst of those who were seated upon costly thrones and arrayed in magnificent attire,
the son of Raghu alone shone with his own splendor, like the Pārijāta tree among the Kalpa trees.
The throngs of eyes of the city-dwellers fell upon him, leaving behind all other kings,
like wild bees deserting flowering trees when a scent-elephant, fierce with rut, has entered the forest.

Then, while the world of kings—descended from the lineages of the Moon and the Sun—was being praised by bards well-versed in genealogy, and while incense produced from the essence of agallochum was being wafted, perfuming the mass of banners with its plumes; ||| Ragh(K)_6.8 |||

When the conch shells were blown and the sound of musical instruments, intended for auspicious purposes, swelled in all directions, it became the cause for the peacocks dwelling in the groves on the outskirts of the city to break into vigorous dances.

Mounted upon a four-sided palanquin carried by men, adorned by a retinue of maidens, and dressed in garments mixed with festive ornaments, the maiden who was to choose her own husband entered the royal highway between the rows of platforms.
At that extraordinary creation of the Creator, consisting of a maiden and the object of a thousand eyes,
the lords of men fell with their inner hearts, remaining on their seats only by means of their bodies.

Various amorous gestures of the kings, whose desires were clearly manifested toward her, became the foremost messengers of their affection, just as the beauty of a gentle breeze is the precursor to the blossoming of trees.
With both hands, someone whirled a play-lotus whose stalk was firmly grasped, which struck bees with its trembling petals,
and which shone with a halo of pollen within.

Another graceful man, turning his handsome face slightly to one side, lifted his upper garment— which had slipped from his shoulder and momentarily caught on the edge of his armlet— and adjusted it back to its proper place.
Then another, with the tips of his fingers slightly curled and the beauty of his eyes somewhat cast down,
scratched the golden footstool with a foot whose nail-lustre was mingled with the rays of jewels.

Another, resting his left arm—adorned with heavy bracelets—at the edge of the seat by pressing it against his side, had his necklace displaced as his waist twisted; he became intent on conversing with a friend.

Another youth tore with the tips of his nails a pale ketaka petal, serving as a decorative ear-ornament for a playful woman, using them as if they were the very marks left by the contact of his beloved’s hips.
With a hand whose palm was copper-red like a lotus and marked with the sign of a banner,
he gracefully moved the dice, which were illuminated by the radiance of his shining rings.
One [of them], although remaining in his assigned place, as if transgressing his own station,
extended a hand whose fingers were filled with rays of diamonds toward the crown.
Then Sunandā, the guardian of the inner apartments, who was as eloquent as a man and well-versed in the learning, conduct, and lineages of kings,
led the princess into the presence of the Lord of Magadha and spoke to her.
He was a refuge for those seeking protection, possessed of unfathomable courage, established in Magadha,
a king who had won renown by delighting his subjects, named Parantapa— a name truly significant of his character.
Granted that there are kings by the thousands, yet they say this earth possesses a true king only because of him;
for though a night is crowded with constellations, stars, and planets, it is radiant only through the moon.

Through the continuous performance of sacrifices, he who had been incessantly invoked by the thousand-eyed Indra caused Śacī’s curls— once hanging over her pale cheeks— to remain for a long time devoid of mandāra flowers.
If you desire that your hand be taken by this most excellent groom during his entrance,
then provide a festival for the eyes of the women of Puṣpapura as they lean from the windows of the palaces.

When she had spoken thus, the slender maiden, her garland of *madhūka* flowers and *dūrvā* grass slightly loosened as she looked at him, rebuked him by means of a simple act of salutation alone, remaining silent.
Then, the woman appointed to carry the cane led the princess to another king,
just as a line of waves stirred by the wind leads a royal swan of Lake Mānasa from one lotus to another.

And this lord of men, whose youthful splendor was craved by celestial nymphs and who, according to the authors of the Sūtras, occupies the portion of humility while enjoying the status of Indra even though he dwells upon the earth, spoke to her.
By shedding teardrops as large as pearls upon their breasts,
he provided the wives of his enemies with necklaces, even without the strings to fasten them.
In this world, Fortune and Sarasvatī— whose natural abodes are distinct yet who dwell together here—
have you alone as their third, O auspicious lady, worthy of them by virtue of your beauty, your speech, and your truthful nature.
Then, averting her gaze from the King of Aṅga, the princess said to her companions, "Let us go.
It was not that he was undesirable, nor that she did not know how to see him properly; for people have diverse tastes.
Then, the female doorkeeper stationed at the entrance presented to him King Duṣprasaha, who was difficult for enemies to withstand and exceptionally handsome,
like the newly risen moon to Indumatī.
This lord of Avanti, with his uplifted arms, broad chest, and slender, rounded waist,
shines like the sun fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ on a lathe, having been whirled around upon a wheel.
In his expeditions, the dust raised by the leading horses of that sovereign ruler of complete power causes the setting of the sprouting rays of light from the crest-jewels of his subordinate vassals.
Dwelling not far from the abode of Mahākāla, whose crown is adorned with the crescent moon,
he enjoys the pleasures of touch with his female companions even during the day through the moonlight filtering through the lattice windows.
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, do you perhaps take pleasure in the mind of this young king in wandering through the series of gardens shaken by the breezes from the waves of the Siprā?
Even toward that reflection whose form was radiant and who had dried up the mire of his enemies with his majesty,
she— possessing unsurpassed delicacy— did not fix her affection, just as the night-lotus does not feel attachment for the sun.
Having placed before her that girl of beautiful nose— who shone like the interior of a lotus, who was not inferior in virtues to the king of Anūpa,
and who was a graceful creation of the Creator— Sunandā spoke once more.
It is said that the yogi Kārtavīrya possessed a thousand arms won in battle, had erected sacrificial posts throughout the eighteen islands,
and held the title of "King" which was not shared by any other.
Simultaneously with the very thought of improper action, the wielder of the bow appeared before him;
he who, as the subduer of men, even within their own bodies, had already restrained their lack of discipline.
In his prison, Daśānana— having conquered Vāsava— dwelt until [Rāma’s] favor was obtained, his arms rendered motionless by the binding of the bowstring and his rows of mouths sighing incessantly.
In his lineage was born this king named Pradīpa, a servant of the elders learned in the scriptures,
by whom the ill repute that the Goddess of Fortune is "naturally fickle" and thus prone to the fault of shifting her residence has been wiped away.
Having obtained as his ally in battle Kṛṣṇagati, who is the night of destruction for the kṣatriyas,
he regards the sharp edge of Paraśurāma’s axe as having the delicacy of a lotus petal.

O you whose beauty is like that of the digit of the moon, become the wife of this long-armed king if you have the desire to behold the river Revā, which is as lovely as a braid of water, with its banks girdled by the hips of the walls of Māhiṣmatī and its waters shimmering through the lattices of its palaces.
Although his appearance was exceedingly pleasing, that lord of the earth did not bring her delight,
just as the full moon, its crimson hue washed away by the autumnal clouds, fails to please the night-lily.

The maiden was addressed by the female guardian of the inner apartments regarding Suṣeṇa, the lord of the Śūrasenas, whose fame was sung in other lands and who was a lamp illuminating both his lineages through purity of conduct.

This king is of the Nīpa lineage and a performer of sacrifices; by relying upon his virtues, even natural enmity was cast aside by [his subjects] as if they had reached the peaceful hermitage of the Siddhas.
In his own body, there was a splendor as delightful to the eyes as that of the moon;
yet in the palaces of his enemies, his unbearable brilliance blazed even among the sprouts of grass grown upon the rooftops of their mansions.
At the time of his water-sports, because of the washing away of the sandalwood paste from the breasts of the women in his harem,
the Yamunā— even though she had reached Mathurā— shone as if her waters were mingled with the waves of the Gaṅgā.
He, who— having been saved from Tārkṣya by Kāliya, the inhabitant of the Yamunā— wears the jewel surrendered by him,
which spreads its luster across his chest and seems to put to shame Kṛṣṇa along with his Kaustubha gem.
O beautiful one, having won this youth as your husband, enjoy the splendor of your youth in Vṛndāvana— which is no less than the Caitraratha grove— upon flower-beds spread over soft young shoots.
And having occupied the stone slabs covered with mica and sprinkled with droplets of water,
behold the dance of peacocks in the lovely caves of Govardhana during the rainy season.
With her charming navel like a whirlpool, she— who was destined to become the wife of another— passed by that king,
just as a river flowing toward the ocean passes a mountain encountered on its course.

Then a maidservant spoke to the young woman, whose face was like the full moon, as she approached the Lord of Kaliṅga named Hemāṅgada— his arms embraced by Aṅgada, who had subdued the factions of his enemies.
This lord of Mahendra and the great ocean, whose strength is equal to Mount Mahendra,
appears as if Mahendra himself were marching before him on his expeditions under the guise of the rutting elephants of his army.
That one of noble arms, the foremost among archers, bears upon his two arms the scars from the bowstring—
scars that appear like the two tracks of the captive Fortune of his enemies, as if moistened by tears mixed with collyrium.
From the lattices of his palace in his own abode, Yama beholds the ocean— whose rows of palm trees on the shore appear like a curtain—
and it awakens him as he sleeps, its deep roar putting to rest the drums that signal the end of the watches.
Dwelling with him on the shores of the ocean, rustling with groves of palm trees,
you shall have the drops of perspiration removed by breezes carrying the fragrance of clove blossoms brought from other islands.
Although thus awakened, the younger sister of the King of Vidarbha, whose form was so alluring,
turned away from him as if Fortune herself were led away by human effort despite adverse destiny.

Then a female door-keeper, approaching the lord of Nāgapura who was like a god in appearance, spoke to the daughter of Bhoja, who possessed the beauty of a Naga woman: "O lady with eyes like those of a cakora bird, look this way! *Raghuvamśa* 6.59.
This Pāṇḍya king, with long necklaces resting upon his shoulders and his body anointed with yellow sandalwood paste,
shines like the king of mountains, whose peaks are reddened by the morning sun and from which waterfalls are gushing forth.

Agastya, the one who brought the great mountain Vindhya to a standstill and who drank and then released the lord of the oceans without remainder, becomes his personal priest at the ceremonial bath (*sauasnātika*) out of affection for him whose body is still moist from the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice.
By him, who had obtained from Hara a weapon difficult to acquire,
the haughty Lord of Laṅkā, fearing a crushing of Janasthāna in the past, set out after forming an alliance for the sake of conquering Indra’s realm.

Now that he, of noble lineage, has taken your hand according to the prescribed rite, become the co-wife of the Southern Quarter— whose girdle is the ocean studded with jewels— and be as weighty as the Earth herself.

Be pleased to sport forever upon the plateaus of the Malaya mountains, where areca palms are entwined with betel vines, sandalwood trees are embraced by cardamom creepers, and the ground is strewn with the leaves of the *tamāla*.
This king has a body dark as the blue lotus, while you have a slender form fair as yellow pigment;
may your union be like that of lightning and a rain-cloud, for the mutual enhancement of your beauty.
That instruction of his found no entry into the heart of his father-in-law, the lord of Vidarbha,
just as a ray of the moon finds no place in a lotus that has closed its petals due to the absence of the sun.
Like the flickering flame of a lamp at night, as that maiden choosing her husband passed by one after another,
each king fell into a state of pallor, like a turret on a royal highway in the dark.
When she appeared before him, the son of Raghu was overwhelmed with doubt as to whether he should choose her or not;
but his right arm dispelled his uncertainty by the throbbing of its armlet-fastenings.
Having obtained him, whose every limb was faultless, the princess desisted from approaching others;
for a swarm of bees, having reached a blossoming mango tree, does not long for another tree.
Perceiving that Indumatī, whose radiance was like the moon, had fixed her mental faculties entirely upon him,
Sunandā, who knew the proper sequence of events, proceeded to speak these words in great detail.
Born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, he was the preeminent peak among kings, Kakutstha by name, endowed with auspicious marks;
from him the lords of Uttarakosala, their aspirations lofty, have borne the praiseworthy title of Kākutstha.
Having mounted the great bull as Mahendra,
he who assumed the playful role of Pinākin in battle rendered the cheeks of the asura women devoid of decorative leaf-designs with his arrows.

He who, rubbing his own armlet against the armlet of Indra as he approached, took half the throne of the Destroyer of Mountains, even though Indra’s armlet was loosened by the striking of Airāvaṇa; he, though possessing the foremost form himself, occupied the seat of the god who cleaves the mountains.
Born into that family of Indukīrti was King Dilīpa, a lamp for his lineage,
who stopped short of the ninety-nine sacrifices in order to avoid provoking the jealousy of Śakra.

While he ruled the earth, even the wind did not disarrange the silken garments of proud women who had fallen asleep halfway to their pleasure-grounds; so who would have ventured to reach out a hand to steal their ornaments?

His son, Rāghava, now rules his station; he is the performer of the great Viśvajit sacrifice, who reduced all royal fortune—accumulated by the submission of the four quarters—to nothing more than the remains of an earthen vessel.
His fame— having ascended the mountains, crossed the oceans, entered the abode of serpents,
and reached the heights— is such that no one is able to measure its extent.
That prince, born after his elder brother like Jayanta born after Indra,
the lord of heaven, is a disciplined youth who, like a draft-ox, bears the heavy ancestral yoke of the world with equal strength.
By virtue of your lineage, beauty, youth, and those various qualities preeminent in discipline, choose him who is your equal; let this jewel be united with gold.
Then, at the conclusion of Sunandā’s speech, the princess, softening her shame,
welcomed the prince with a glance pure with favor, as if with a garland of choice.
Due to her modesty, she was unable to express her bond of longing for that youth;
yet, through the visible sign of horripilation, it emerged from the slender body of the fair-haired maiden, piercing through her very frame.
